source: Carey, Tanaka & van der Meer (2019) Reward revaluation biases hippocampal replay content away from the preferred outcome (bioRxiv preprint full text)
finding: Rats chose between food (left) and water (right) on a T-maze, with food or water restriction on alternate days. Sharp-wave-ripple content was biased toward the arm that was NOT preferred that day, including before the day's task started. Replay content was anticorrelated with choice.
numbers: 4 rats, 19 of 24 sessions analysed (>=40 cells). Choice 89% food on food-restricted days, 80% water on water-restricted days. Sequenceless decoding: motivation improved mixed model, LR=10.1, p=.0015; SWR content z=-.41 (food-restricted) vs +.40 (water-restricted), p=.004; choice vs content r(19)=-.75, p<.001. Sequence decoding: left-arm proportion .35 vs .57, p=.038. Pre-task bias z=-.55 vs .39, p=.003. Day n-1 behaviour did not predict day n content (r=-.11, p=.65).
quote: biased away from the preferred outcome
limits: Only 4 rats, uneven sessions. SWR content did not predict trial-by-trial choice beyond motivation in a way that proves it drives behaviour; overtrained animals may not use hippocampus. Within-session experience simulations did not reproduce the bias. Read from the preprint, not the journal version; last 24k characters unread.
agent_relevance: Directly limits a plain replay-what-you-will-choose-next reading. Replay of the non-preferred option is compatible with a gain term (the non-preferred option is where a policy change could come from) but not with a need-only or recency rule. Keep a rule that revisits the option the agent currently disfavours.

source: Gagne & Dayan (2022) Optimism and pessimism in optimised replay, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: Extends Mattar and Daw gain x need to agents that forget. When the internal model is uncertain because of forgetting, optimal replay should favour sub-optimal actions the agent wrongly chose, so pessimal replay is rational. The authors fit this to individual human subjects (re-analysis of the Eldar 2020 MEG data) and suggest it can account for Carey-type pessimal replay.
numbers: Human data: MEG sequenceness; n=25 subjects with non-negligible sequenceness; sequenceness vs probability of policy change, Spearman M=0.04, SEM=0.02, p=0.04 (bootstrap). Model forgetting parameter vs decision flexibility in the flexible group: beta=-0.37, t=-2.73, p=0.016. Gain threshold vs objective replay benefit: beta=0.24, p=0.083 (n.s.).
limits: Fits are to one human dataset; the effect is small (M=0.04). A reviewer questioned assumptions. The rat result is explained by analogy, not fitted to Carey's data. This is a model with forgetting, not a test of an ordering rule.
agent_relevance: Closes part of the Carey gap: gain-based replay can predict replay of disfavoured options when the model is uncertain. For an LLM, a stale or uncertain stored belief should raise, not lower, the case for revisiting it.

source: Jensen, Hennequin & Mattar (2024) A recurrent network model of planning explains hippocampal replay and human behavior, Nat Neurosci
finding: A recurrent RL agent can meta-learn WHEN to run a policy rollout (a replay-like simulation) instead of acting. Its rollouts help in the same situations where humans think longer, and resemble rat forward replay.
numbers: 94 Prolific participants, 4x4 periodic maze, 40 episodes of 20 s. Agent rollout probability vs human thinking time: Pearson r=0.186 +/- 0.007 (mean +/- s.e.m. across participants; chance 0 +/- 0.004); after conditioning on distance to goal r=0.070 +/- 0.006. Forcing more rollouts cut actions to goal monotonically up to at least 15 rollouts; with no feedback from the rollout to the network the effect was much weaker. 5 trained agents.
limits: Correlations are small. Rollouts are sampled from the agent's own policy; the paper does not compute gain x need and has no uncertainty-aware value of a rollout. It does not fix the myopic limit by theory; it sidesteps it by learning when to plan.
agent_relevance: Support for learned, state-dependent triggering of simulation as a cheaper stand-in for a hand-built utility. For an LLM scaffold: decide when to revisit from features (new information, distance to goal), and test it against a fixed schedule.

source: Diekmann & Cheng (2023) A model of hippocampal replay driven by experience and environmental structure facilitates spatial learning, eLife
finding: A cheap stochastic replay rule using three variables (experience strength, similarity, inhibition of return) trains RL agents far better than random replay and comes close to Mattar and Daw's costly algorithm.
numbers: Abstract only: far better than random replay; close to the Mattar and Daw algorithm. No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Spatial tasks, tabular-style agents.
agent_relevance: A cheap proxy can recover most of gain x need. Candidate cheap rule for an agent: strength (how often a subgoal mattered) + similarity to the current state + inhibition of return (do not revisit the same item twice in a row).

source: Wimmer, Liu, McNamee & Dolan (2023) Distinct replay signatures for prospective decision-making and memory preservation, PNAS
finding: Human MEG replay has two roles in one task. Before choice, replay of the current environment was stronger when model-based planning paid off. After reward, replay of the alternative (distal) environment was stronger the longer since it was last experienced.
numbers: Abstract only; sample size and statistics not read.
limits: Abstract only. Human MEG, one task.
agent_relevance: Replay priority tracks need before action and lower recency after feedback. That is the opposite of a pure recency rule after feedback. Suggests a quota for the least recently visited items (K07).

source: Chen, Zhao, Wang, Yang, Zhang & Niu (2024/2025) Enhancing LLM Agents for Code Generation with Possibility and Pass-rate Prioritized Experience Replay (P2Value, BTP pipeline), arXiv 2410.12236
finding: P2Value = alpha x model probability + (1-alpha) x test pass rate, used to rank failed programs for replay during fine-tuning (rank-based priority p_i = 1/rank). The paper reports gains, but the large numbers come from fine-tuning small models on programs sampled by a stronger model. It has no ablation of priority ordering versus uniform replay in the text read, so ordering and filtering are not separated.
numbers: APPS mixed, pass rate / accuracy: GPT-Neo base 5.73 / 3.31 -> fine-tuned on GPT-4-turbo samples 42.12 / 20.54. Self-fine-tuning (Table 2) is small: GPT-2 7.30 -> 8.12 pass, 2.72 -> 3.92 accuracy; GPT-Neo 5.73 -> 5.39 pass (down), 3.31 -> 3.72; WizardCoder 40.24 -> 41.25 pass. GPT-4-turbo itself scores 81.25 pass on APPS mixed. Table label alignment in the PDF text is messy, so row pairing is read from the layout.
limits: Large gain is mostly distillation from a stronger model, not replay ordering. Self-improvement gains are within noise and one is negative. Authors say tasks with few tests give pass rates near zero and hurt the method. Appendix ablations on alpha not read. Training-time method.
agent_relevance: K14 headline numbers now extracted: do not cite P2Value as evidence that ordering by priority helps. Treat as unverified for ordering.

source: Li et al. (2026) DyJR: Preserving Local Policy Plasticity in RLVR via Dynamic Jensen-Shannon Replay, arXiv 2603.16157 (NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Separates who is admitted to the replay buffer from how replay is used. Confidence-based admission and JS regularisation each help; a short recency window helps; a long history hurts. Uses replay as a regulariser against collapse, not as ordering.
numbers: Six math benchmarks, Qwen3-4B-Base: GRPO 29.8 -> DyJR 34.1 (+4.3); Ex-GRPO 32.6; RLEP 31.8; 3 independent runs for GRPO, DyJR, RLEP, Ex-GRPO. Qwen3-1.7B: 17.3 -> 19.5. Matched controls: confidence admission +2.5 points for PG+IS, +3.7 for JS; with admission fixed JS adds +1.5 over PG+IS (0.3 under perfect-only admission). Recency window M=8 -> 16, 32, 64: 34.1 -> 32.9, 31.7, 30.9. Static reference + JS 31.7; reverse-KL 29.4; forward-KL 32.5; entropy regularisation 29.7. SQL BIRD/Spider Pass@1 +3.3/+5.0.
limits: Ablations are single-run; the paper itself says they do not establish significance. Filtering by confidence, not ranking by utility. Training-time.
agent_relevance: K15 answered: the lift decomposes into admission (filter), recency (freshness), and use. A scaffold analogue: cap the age of a stored item and filter before ordering. Also shows older anchors lose value (ties to staleness).

source: Ma et al. (2026) Freshness-Aware Prioritized Experience Replay for LLM/VLM RL (FreshPER), arXiv 2604.16918
finding: Priority staleness is the failure mode. Exponential age decay w_age = exp(-age/tau) is derived from effective sample size, which decays exponentially with policy divergence. The best tau depends on how fast the policy drifts.
numbers: tau=500 best on Sokoban Simple (fast drift), tau=1000 on FrozenLake (slower); half-life = tau x ln 2. Standard PER without decay underperforms on-policy on most tasks and fails badly on Sokoban Simple and NQ Search. Peak gains +46% NQ Search, +367% Sokoban Simple, +133% VLM FrozenLake; little gain on CliffWalking and GSM8K.
limits: Training-time RL over gradient steps, not a reasoning episode. tau tuned per task. Eight tasks, single settings.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6 only by analogy: decay should be faster when the situation changes faster. For a reasoning episode, tie decay to events (new evidence arrives) rather than to a clock; no study measures that directly.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory, arXiv 2601.03192
finding: Closest direct hit on gap 1. A frozen LLM keeps episodic memories with a learned Q-value (expected utility from environment reward). Retrieval is two-phase: similarity top-k1, then re-rank by a mix of similarity and Q. It beats similarity-only RAG and memory baselines. This is learned outcome utility, not gain x need, and no recency or random ordering control at equal tokens is in the main table.
numbers: Table 1 average last-epoch/CSR: No memory 0.631; RAG 0.679/0.699; Self-RAG 0.673/0.726; Mem0 0.681/0.712; MemP 0.736/0.760; MemRL 0.772/0.798 (+3.8% CSR over MemP). Benchmarks: BigCodeBench (GPT-4o), Lifelong Agent Bench OS and DB (GPT-4o-mini), ALFWorld (GPT-5-mini), HLE (Gemini-3-pro). Transfer: +2.8% over MemP; ALFWorld +5.8%. Q weight lambda in {0,.25,.5,.75,1}: concave, peak at 0.5; pure similarity (0) plateaus, lambda near 1 is volatile (figure only). k1=5, k2=3 best; denser (10/5) hurts. Learned Q vs empirical success: Pearson r=0.861; success 21.5% in lowest Q bin to 88.1% in highest. About 12% of high-Q memories were failure memories.
limits: Different benchmarks use different models, so the average mixes models. Single runs, no confidence intervals seen. The Q-critic needs reward feedback over 10 epochs of repeated tasks, so it is not available inside one reasoning episode. Table 3 shows much of the gain comes from cross-task retrieval (+9.0% OS, +5.1% ALFWorld vs single-task).
agent_relevance: Evidence that ordering stored items by learned utility beats similarity alone. Missing for us: a no-reward proxy and a within-episode version. Closes part of gap 1 (utility ordering exists), leaves the equal-tokens recency/random control open.

source: Kang et al. (2026) Learning What to Remember: Observability-Safe Memory Retention (OSL-MR), arXiv 2606.10616
finding: Compares retention policies under a memory budget on LoCoMo and LongMemEval. A baseline that asks the LLM to rate importance (Generative Agents style, GA-LLM) is no better than plain recency. A mixed heuristic and a learned policy are better.
numbers: LoCoMo F1, budget 32: Recency 0.017, GA-heuristic 0.019, GA-LLM 0.016, Mixed-Score 0.057, BC-learner 0.090, OSL-MR 0.123. Budget 64: Recency 0.022, GA-LLM 0.020, Mixed-Score 0.077, BC 0.167, OSL-MR 0.239. Budget 128: OSL-MR precision 0.201, recall 0.561, F1 0.263; Mixed-Score F1 0.087; Recency and GA F1 below 0.03. Means over cross-validation folds with SD reported; OSL-MR best in every fold.
limits: This is retention (what to keep), not retrieval order. Preprint (v6). The authors built the Mixed-Score and the learner, so they are not neutral. Budget is a count of memories, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 evidence: an LLM self-rated importance score (the cheap proxy most scaffolds use) did not beat recency here. A proxy mixing recency, overlap with the current question, and learned evidence did. Do not trust self-rated importance without a control.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior, arXiv 2304.03442
finding: Memory retrieval scores each memory by recency, importance and relevance. Importance is a self-rated integer 1 to 10 from the LLM (how poignant). Its ablations remove observation, reflection and planning access, not the importance or recency terms, so the proxy itself is untested.
numbers: Believability ranking (TrueSkill): full architecture top; the next ablation, no reflection, had mu=22.95 (sigma=0.69). Retrieval weights all set to 1 in the implementation; scores min-max scaled to [0,1].
limits: Interview-based evaluation with 100 crowdworkers; no ablation of retrieval-score terms. Only the scoring section and ablation list were read closely.
agent_relevance: Shows the self-rated importance proxy is the field default but was never validated against true benefit. Combined with d10 it is a weak proxy.

source: Janner, Fu, Zhang & Levine (2019) When to Trust Your Model: Model-Based Policy Optimization (MBPO), arXiv 1906.08253
finding: Answer to gap 9 for Dyna-style agents. Compounding model error grows with rollout length (the bound scales with the square of the effective horizon). MBPO branches short rollouts from real states instead of full model rollouts, which keeps error bounded and matches model-free asymptotic performance with fewer samples.
numbers: Best schedule on Hopper raised rollout length k linearly from 1 to 15; fixing k=1 also worked well. Theorem 4.2 gives a bound with one term falling exponentially in k and one rising linearly in k.
limits: Continuous control with learned neural dynamics, not language. Rollout length schedule tuned.
agent_relevance: For an agent that simulates its own continuations: start simulations from real, checked states and keep them short. Re-ground often.

source: Panahi, Patterson, White & White (2024) Investigating the Interplay of Prioritized Replay and Generalization, RLC 2024, arXiv 2407.09702
finding: Prioritisation helps value propagation in tabular settings. With neural networks it produces error spikes, and in control tasks no prioritised variant consistently beats uniform replay, even with delayed target updates or expected-TD-error estimates.
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers read.
limits: Abstract and intro lines only; full text not read. Deep RL, not language.
agent_relevance: Strengthens K10: ordering by error is brittle once a learned function generalises across items, as an LLM does. Always keep a uniform control.

source: Aubin et al. (2018) Prioritized Sweeping Neural DynaQ with Multiple Predecessors, and Hippocampal Replays, arXiv 1802.05594
finding: A neural prioritised-sweeping Dyna-Q learner with multiple predecessors improves simulated navigation and predicts that rest-period replays should be shuffled.
numbers: Search listing only: no numbers.
limits: Listing only.
agent_relevance: Earlier neural prioritised sweeping with a replay link; weak background for gaps 9 and 7.

source: Pham & Dam (2026) Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning, arXiv 2609.06186
finding: Adds a graph-diffusion term to the Bellman-residual priority for nonstationary rewards, scheduled by the spectral gap. A 2026 repair for stale priority when rewards change.
numbers: Listing only: tested on FourRooms and GARNET; no numbers.
limits: Listing only.
agent_relevance: Relevant to gap 6: nonstationary reward is the same problem as the situation changing mid-episode. Numbers not read, so not citable yet.

source: Brea (2017) Is prioritized sweeping the better episodic control?, arXiv 1711.06677
finding: In deterministic tree MDPs, episodic control matches prioritised sweeping. In general environments prioritised sweeping does better even with equal resource limits.
numbers: Listing only: no numbers.
limits: Listing only. Tabular.
agent_relevance: Equal-resource comparison of priority-based backup against recall-by-similarity, the closest classical analogue to gap 1.

source: 2026 LLM step-credit papers (search-listing summaries only): SRPO arXiv 2605.25507; FOCUS arXiv 2610.35801; TTEL arXiv 2607.21453
finding: Many 2026 LLM papers do step-level credit assignment, localise errors, or reset to an earlier step. None found compares revisiting steps in reverse versus forward order at equal tokens. TTEL reports pass@64 of 71.0% with 360.4k tokens vs 735.0k for independent sampling by localising the error.
numbers: FOCUS: 55.4 vs 48.2 BrowseComp-Plus (+7.2), 56.5 vs 52.4 DeonticBench (+4.1), selective-branching critic vs GRPO. TTEL: Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench. All from search-page summaries only.
limits: Listing text only; none opened. The ordering question (reverse vs forward) is not what these test.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. The nearest evidence is that localising and revisiting the faulty step beats resampling from scratch (TTEL), which is a gain-style choice of where to revisit.

source: Liu et al. (2021) Experience replay is associated with efficient nonlocal learning, Science: forward-citation check via Europe PMC
finding: Searched Europe PMC for papers citing Liu 2021 (128 citing records) and for titles combining replay, human participants, gain and need. Found extensions of human MEG replay (Wimmer 2023, Jensen 2024) but no direct replication or larger-sample re-test of the gain-beats-need result.
numbers: 128 citing records; top items are reviews, Wimmer 2023 (PNAS), Jensen 2024, Diekmann 2023. No replication title found.
limits: Search is by title and keyword only; Europe PMC misses preprints and non-biomedical venues. Absence of a hit is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Treat the gain-over-need human result as one study (N=29).

source: Mattar & Daw (2018) forward-citation scan for non-myopic or uncertainty-aware replay value (Europe PMC, 92 citing records 2024-2026)
finding: Scanned 2019-2026 citers. Theory extensions found: Gagne & Dayan 2022 (uncertainty and forgetting, pessimal replay), Jensen 2024 (learned when-to-plan), Diekmann & Cheng 2023 (cheap proxy). No paper found that replaces the one-step (myopic) gain with a multi-step value of a replay chain.
numbers: Counts only: 92 citing records in 2024-2026; keyword filter for uncertainty with value/utility/optimal/normative in the title = 0 hits.
limits: Title filters are crude. A non-myopic version may exist under other words or in preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: the uncertainty limit is addressed by d02; the myopic limit stays open. In practice, apply gain to chains of items (a subgoal plus its dependents), not single items, until tested.

source: Yoo, Park, Jang, Kim & Yoon (2026) Rollout-Level Advantage-Prioritized Experience Replay for GRPO, arXiv 2606.04560
finding: Gives an ordering ablation for rollout replay: with replay volume held equal, choosing rollouts by absolute advantage beats choosing them uniformly. Naive replay (uniform or group-level priority) gave no consistent gain over GRPO and fell below it at 4B.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B-Base, five math benchmarks, Table 4 (single seed): rollout-level uniform replay 16.19 avg / 28.96 pass; |A| priority 16.58 / 32.35 (gap +0.39 avg, +3.39 pass); query-level group priority 15.43 / 29.04. Main results (3 seeds): gain over GRPO +0.61 pp (0.6B), +0.60 (1.7B), +1.66 (4B). At 4B naive replay was 0.83 and 1.82 pp below no-replay GRPO. Age cap max=10 gave pass 32.35; max=1 29.59; max=30 27.34; max=60 26.66.
quote: Naive replay gives no consistent gain over GRPO under either uniform or g priority
limits: Ablations are single seed; authors say the uniform control does not show equal accuracy is unreachable by spending the same compute on generation; training-time replay, not prompt-time ordering; fresh-anchored composition and age eviction are part of the recipe.
agent_relevance: First clean priority-vs-uniform control at equal replay count in LLM RL. Supports ordering by learning signal, and shows a staleness cap (about 10 steps) matters. Still training, not a scaffold.

source: Chen & Cheng (2026) Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory, arXiv 2606.12945
finding: Gives recency, random and single-cue controls for value-ranked memory at a fixed keep budget. A learned multi-factor value kept far more gold evidence than recency, which was only a little above random. A cue that scores relevance to the future question works only when the question is known (oracle) and falls to near chance when it is not.
numbers: LongMemEval-S, 479 usable cases, keep top 30% of turns, 20 resampled 50/50 splits. Blind gold retention: learned 0.770+-0.011; uniform weights 0.657; self-relevance only 0.518; reliability only 0.497; recency only 0.368+-0.021; random 0.300; goal-only 0.286; emotion only 0.201. Oracle regime (goal relevance scored against the held-out question): goal-only 0.979, learned 0.993. Learned weights: reliability 0.64, self/user 0.23, goal 0.00. Bootstrap 95% CIs above zero for every paired gap.
quote: scoring goal relevance against the held-out evaluation question (an oracle that peeks at the future query) saturates
limits: Retention (keep or drop), not revisit order; no answerer run, so no QA accuracy; budget equal by construction; factors are LLM-annotated cues; preprint by small-organisation authors.
agent_relevance: A value score beat recency at fixed budget, and a need cue must not use information from the future question. Recency (0.368) barely beat random (0.300), so recency is a weak default.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) Credit Assignment with Resets in Language Model Reasoning (RRPO and SRPO), arXiv 2605.25507
finding: The model returns to the first step it judges wrong and resamples from there (a gain-like choice of which state to revisit) or to a random step. Self-chosen reset beat random reset and plain GRPO; the quality of the choice drives the benefit.
numbers: OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, 10 benchmarks, 3 seeds, 8 rollouts per prompt (compute matched). SRPO best on 7/10 tasks (14B) and 6/10 (7B); RRPO about equal to GRPO. LiveCodeBench v6 medium, 383 problems, chains of about 17 thoughts. Clean-prefix resets corrected 28.7% vs 16.3% Pass@4 for resets in the erroneous region (nearly 2x). Split 1 base group + 4 suffixes from one prefix won most columns over 2 prefixes x 4 and 1 x 8.
limits: Reset to first error is a backward target, but this is not a test of backward vs forward order; training-time RL; localisation graded against Claude Opus 4.5; about half of self-localisations overshoot into erroneous steps.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of 'revisit the high-gain state': spend the revisit where a better action exists. Self-rated 'first wrong step' is a usable but imperfect gain proxy. Backward-vs-forward at equal tokens stays untested.

source: Wu et al. (2026) STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid? arXiv 2605.06527
finding: Tests what happens when a later message silently invalidates a stored belief, directly (Type I) or through a dependency (Type II). Models and memory frameworks mostly fail; propagated cases are harder; a write-time propagation search helps a lot.
numbers: 400 scenarios, 1,200 queries, contexts up to 150K tokens, three probes (State Resolution, Premise Resistance, Implicit Policy Adaptation). Best plain model (Gemini-3.1-pro) 55.2% overall; memory frameworks 5.1% to 17.8% overall; CUPMEM (propagation-aware search) 68.0% overall, premise resistance 78.0% (Type I) and 75.0% (Type II) against near zero for most baselines. Type II lower than Type I in nearly all systems.
limits: Table row labels were shifted in text extraction, so per-model rows are not trusted; headline figures from abstract and body text. No recency-vs-dependency retrieval ablation. CUPMEM costs about $0.37 per instance.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that stale beliefs dominate failure after a changed fact and that revisiting dependants of the changed item (non-myopic scope) is where gains lie. Supports event-triggered invalidation with dependency search.

source: Dao, Kathalkar & Eaton (2026) Weighted Memory Tree: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon LLM Agents, arXiv 2608.20631
finding: A prompt-level memory with retention scores updated by events (outcome recorded, branch failed or superseded) and decay driven by missed selections, not elapsed time ('Elapsed time alone does not affect retention'). Branch priority scores the whole subtree (max plus mean of its memories minus failed and obsolete fractions). Beats linear history and an unweighted tree.
numbers: GAIA-Text, Qwen3-8B / Gemma 4 E4B / Llama-3.1-8B, accuracy % (prompt tokens M): linear history 20.47 (43.67) / 24.41 (65.27) / 9.45 (73.96); unweighted tree 15.75 (39.24) / 25.20 (53.90) / 9.45 (77.13); full WMT 33.86 (32.48) / 33.07 (37.85) / 17.32 (51.17). Mean gain over linear +9.97 pp with 32.8% fewer prompt tokens. Full GAIA: WMT 29.70 / 30.91 / 24.85.
limits: Small models; GAIA-Text 127 questions; no recency or random control; scoring, folding and suppression are bundled so ordering is not isolated; selector is an LLM; single run per cell; preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest prompt-time scaffold to our memory: event refresh plus decay by missed selection, branch-level (non-myopic) priority, invalidation suppresses. Shows the package helps; does not isolate ordering.

source: Matam & Kim (2026) MemDecay: Region-Aware KV Cache Eviction for Efficient LLM Agent Inference, arXiv 2607.10582
finding: Measured how long parts of an agent prompt stay attended to. Lifetimes differ by about 10x across regions, so one decay constant is wrong. Pure recency retention collapses as context grows while a structural prior keeps working.
numbers: Contexts of about 450 and 1,700 tokens, Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B: system half-lives 148 to 189 decode steps vs 14 to 16 for scratchpad reasoning. Pinning kept system facts at the full-cache ceiling in every setting; no baseline preserved more than 13 of 24. Attention-term ablation: the attention weight could not compensate at any tested weight.
limits: KV-cache eviction in tiny models and short contexts; not note or subgoal ordering; no refresh-vs-decay ablation reported.
agent_relevance: Supports per-type decay constants (plans slow, scratch notes fast) in the schema.

source: Diba & Buzsaki (2007) Forward and reverse hippocampal place-cell sequences during ripples, Nat Neurosci 10:1241-1242 (PMC author manuscript)
finding: Full-text check of the founding counts; closes the second-hand status of the Diba numbers.
numbers: 36% of events significantly forward correlated and 19% significantly reverse correlated (P<6e-10 forward, P<3.5e-3 reverse); ratio about 2 (1.74 to 2.11, 95% CI). 841 of 887 forward events at the start end before running (preplay); 395 of 464 reverse events at the far end after the run.
quote: the majority (841 out of 887, P < 10-190) of positively correlated significant events occurred at the start end of the track
limits: Linear track, few rats; direction defined by rank-order correlation with a place-field template and 500 shuffles per event; forward events outnumber reverse overall.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Mattar and Daw citation. Direction depends on where in the task the event occurs, so let the score decide direction.

source: Pfeiffer & Foster (2013) Hippocampal place-cell sequences depict future paths to remembered goals, Nature 497:74-79 (PMC author manuscript)
finding: Open-field task with 36 possible goal locations in a 2 m x 2 m arena, alternating random foraging (RANDOM) and a fixed reward place (HOME). Sequences before movement run from the current position toward the goal and predict the immediate path, even for novel start-goal pairs.
numbers: 2,028 trajectory events analysed; zero had P above 0.02 under two shuffle tests; 144 to 373 events per session. HOME was over-represented in away events and not explained by occupancy. Rates of ripples and trajectory events did not differ between HOME and RANDOM.
limits: Number of animals not recovered from the text read; other designs find weaker or opposite biases (Gillespie 2021, Carey 2019).
agent_relevance: Source of the forward-need idea (replay toward the current goal). Event rate did not rise with goal importance, only content did.

source: Tirole, Duvelle & Bendor (2026) Time, but not reward, shapes replay-based episodic prioritization, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.06.10.731494
finding: New rat data against pure utility theories. Behavioural state, not reward size, predicted awake replay rate; in sleep the most recent episode was replayed most regardless of reward value. Model: each replay strengthens an episode-specific priority trace that decays with time and can be refreshed by remote replay.
numbers: Five rats; three with enough CA1 cells for decoding. All rats preferred the undiluted over the 1:1 diluted reward. Reward effect on laps run F(1,60.22)=22.479, p<0.001; immobility time at reward sites p=0.08; replay rate fell with time asleep (t=-4.813, p<0.001). Sleep-POST replay dominated by the most recent episode, not the one with the most earlier replay.
limits: Preprint, three decoded animals, novel-environment sequence design; not peer reviewed in this read.
agent_relevance: A decaying priority trace with refresh competes with or adds to gain x need. Fits event-refreshed decay.

source: Human hippocampal ripples prioritize model-based learning (Neuron 2026, doi 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.03.020), Europe PMC record 41962539 (abstract)
finding: Independent extension of the Liu 2021 line with intracranial recordings: after each outcome, ripples carried information about which indirect experience was most valuable to update; longer ripples carried stronger priority signals; high-priority paths got stronger cortical reactivation than low-priority paths.
numbers: 34 epilepsy patients (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only (journal paywalled); how priority was defined was not read. Different modality and task, so an extension, not a strict replication.
agent_relevance: Moves the Liu replication gap from 'none found' to 'partial independent extension at abstract level'.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw et al. (2025) Between planning and map-building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain, Neuron 113:4278-4292
finding: Extends the Mattar and Daw utility to routes toward future as well as current goals, weighted by an estimated probability of future relevance. Replay then looks like planning when the current goal is likely to recur and like map-building when goals are uncertain; explains replay that lags learning of current goals.
numbers: Animals have about ten blocks per goal to estimate the goal distribution; recency-weighted estimates overweight earlier samples. No new numeric fit read.
limits: Theory paper; parts read; no LLM test; qualitative match to prior data.
agent_relevance: Principled fix for 'need only counts the current goal': need = estimated chance an item is useful later, learned from history.

source: Trait anxiety is associated with reduced reward-related replay at rest, Nat Commun 2025, PMC12381021 (abstract)
finding: Human EEG decoding found backward replay for a reward-linked sequence during rest. Its strength fell with trait anxiety and predicted later preference for reward-predictive stimuli. High-anxiety people showed inefficient credit assignment regardless of reward magnitude.
numbers: Abstract level only; high trait anxiety defined as score at least 45; sample size not read.
limits: Abstract only; correlational.
agent_relevance: Another human backward-replay credit-assignment result; no gain x need test.

source: Imagined-rollout LLM planners with grounding (search listings only): Imagine-then-Plan arXiv 2601.08955; GILP (June 2026); arXiv 2606.27483
finding: For the Dyna question in LLMs: Imagine-then-Plan lets the agent choose how far to imagine (training-free and trained versions). GILP uses a small parameterised world model to check LLM rollouts and reports fewer compounding hallucinations. A Jan 2026 paper finds agents often will not call a world-model tool. None was opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Search summaries only.
agent_relevance: Candidates for the compounding-error gap; not usable as evidence yet.

source: Absence check (WebSearch, 8 queries): non-myopic scoring of a subgoal with its dependants, and recency decay vs event refresh ablations in agent memory
finding: Search found no paper that scores a stored item together with its dependants as an expected-value-of-update, and none that ablates recency decay against event-triggered refresh. Nearest are WMT branch priority and STALE propagation search. No paper directly compares backward and forward revisit at equal tokens.
numbers: Absence finding.
limits: Search recall limited; keyword search only; OpenAlex budget was exhausted.
agent_relevance: These questions stay open; test them in our own harness.
